fields.definition: A bass drum resonant (front) head that has no hole or port cut into it, so the head stays a full, intact membrane. Because the shell is sealed, the drum sustains and resonates more, and a microphone cannot be placed inside it.
fields.plain_english: It is the front skin of a kick drum with no hole cut in it. A solid front skin makes the drum ring longer and boom more, and you cannot put a mic inside.
fields.purpose_function: Keeping the front head solid maximizes the drum's natural sustain, low-end resonance, and open tone, giving a fuller sound than a ported head. It is the standard tuned setup when the goal is the drum's full acoustic voice rather than a tight, mic-focused sound.
fields.practical_application: An engineer facing an unported kick must mic it from outside the resonant head or add a boundary or subkick mic, since there is no port to place a mic inside, and often applies light internal muffling to tame the extra ring.
common_mistakes: Assuming a mic can be slid inside an unported kick; with no port, the mic must sit outside the resonant head or a subkick must be used.
Over-muffling with pillows or blankets to kill the extra sustain, which chokes the low end instead of tuning the drum.
Expecting the same tight, punchy attack as a ported kick; the sealed head naturally gives more ring, boom, and sustain.
Cutting a port into the head to fix mic access when the session actually called for the fuller, sealed sound.
scenario_contexts: Jazz or vintage-style sessions where an open, resonant, full-bodied kick tone is wanted.
Recording a kit whose drummer prefers a solid front head, forcing the engineer to mic outside or add a subkick.
Tuning a deep kick for a boomy, long-sustaining low end rather than a tight modern thud.
A live or studio setup where a sealed front head is kept for maximum low-frequency resonance.

sources: Evans / D'Addario technical documentation — Resonant Bass/Kick Drumheads (ported vs non-ported)
Owsinski, The Recording Engineer's Handbook (kick drum front head and mic placement)
Huber & Runstein, Modern Recording Techniques (bass drum miking)
